title: Forms & User Input
description: Learn to collect user data effectively and accessibly. Master every input type, form validation attributes, labels, fieldsets, and the submit flow — the gateway to interactive web applications.
learningObjectives: Build complete forms using the form element and its attributes
Use all major input types: text, email, password, number, date, range, color, file
Distinguish textarea, select, and datalist elements
Add built-in validation with required, min, max, pattern
Write accessible forms with labels, fieldsets, and ARIA

sections.content: How Forms Work

The <form> element is a container that groups related inputs. When submitted, it sends data to a server URL (action) using HTTP GET or POST (method). Every input inside needs a name attribute — that becomes the key when the data is sent.

<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="username">Username:</label>
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username" />
  
  <label for="email">Email:</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" />
  
  <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>
💡 GET appends data to the URL (visible, bookmarkable). POST sends data in the request body (hidden, secure). Always use POST for passwords and sensitive data.
Button Types

Inside a form, <button type='submit'> submits the form, <button type='reset'> clears all fields, and <button type='button'> does nothing by default (used for JavaScript). Always specify the type attribute explicitly.

<button type="submit">Submit Form</button>
<button type="reset">Clear Fields</button>
<button type="button" onclick="validate()">Check</button>

exercises.question: Create a sign-up form with action='/register' method='POST'. Include fields for 'name' (text), 'email' (email), and 'password' (password), each with a label. Add a submit button.
exercises.solution:
<form action="/register" method="POST">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" />
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" />
  <label for="password">Password</label>
  <input type="password" id="password" name="password" />
  <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>
</form>
hints: form needs action and method attributes
Each input needs a name attribute
Link label to input with for and id
exercises.explanation: The form action is where data is sent. method=POST is secure. name attribute identifies each field's value on the server.

sections.content: More Than Just text
HTML5 introduced many specialized input types that automatically handle validation, show platform-appropriate keyboards on mobile, and provide native UI controls — all without JavaScript.

<!-- Contact info -->
<input type="text" placeholder="Your name" />
<input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
<input type="tel" placeholder="+1 555 0100" />
<input type="url" placeholder="https://yoursite.com" />

<!-- Numbers -->
<input type="number" min="1" max="100" step="1" />
<input type="range" min="0" max="100" value="50" />

<!-- Dates and times -->
<input type="date" />
<input type="time" />
<input type="datetime-local" />
<input type="month" />

<!-- Others -->
<input type="color" value="#00ff87" />
<input type="file" accept=".pdf,.docx" />
<input type="checkbox" id="agree" />
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" />
🎯 On mobile, type='email' shows a keyboard with @, type='number' shows a numeric pad, type='date' shows a date picker. Use the right type for a better UX!

examples.title: Event Registration Form
examples.code:
<form>
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required />

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required />

  <label for="date">Preferred Date</label>
  <input type="date" id="date" name="date" />

  <label for="guests">Number of Guests</label>
  <input type="number" id="guests" name="guests" min="1" max="10" />

  <label for="color">Badge Color</label>
  <input type="color" id="color" name="color" value="#6366f1" />

  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
examples.output: A rich registration form with various specialized input types
examples.explanation: Each input type triggers the appropriate UI and validation on both desktop and mobile.

exercises.question: Which input type would you use to let a user pick a value between 0–100 using a slider?
hints: Think about what a slider control does
exercises.explanation: type='range' renders a slider. Combine with min, max, and step attributes. type='number' shows a text box with up/down arrows.

sections.content: Dropdown Menus with select & option
<select> creates a dropdown list. Each <option> is a choice. The value attribute is what gets sent to the server; the text content is what the user sees. Use <optgroup> to group related options.

<label for="country">Country</label>
<select id="country" name="country">
  <option value="">-- Select a country --</option>
  <optgroup label="Americas">
    <option value="us">United States</option>
    <option value="ca">Canada</option>
  </optgroup>
  <optgroup label="Europe">
    <option value="uk">United Kingdom</option>
    <option value="de">Germany</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>
textarea — Multi-line Text

<label for="message">Message</label>
<textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" cols="40"
  placeholder="Write your message here..."></textarea>
datalist — Autocomplete Suggestions
<datalist> provides autocomplete suggestions for a text input while still allowing free-form text. It's linked to an input via the list attribute.

<label for="framework">Favourite Framework</label>
<input type="text" id="framework" list="frameworks" />
<datalist id="frameworks">
  <option value="React" />
  <option value="Vue" />
  <option value="Angular" />
  <option value="Svelte" />
</datalist>

exercises.question: Create a feedback form with a <select> for rating (options: Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor), a <textarea> for comments (5 rows), and a submit button.
exercises.solution:
<form>
  <label for="rating">Rating</label>
  <select id="rating" name="rating">
    <option value="excellent">Excellent</option>
    <option value="good">Good</option>
    <option value="fair">Fair</option>
    <option value="poor">Poor</option>
  </select>
  <label for="comments">Comments</label>
  <textarea id="comments" name="comments" rows="5"></textarea>
  <button type="submit">Submit Feedback</button>
</form>
exercises.explanation: select is for choosing from a fixed list. textarea is for multi-line free-form text. Both need name attributes to submit their values.

sections.content: Native HTML5 Validation
HTML5 provides powerful built-in validation that runs before form submission — no JavaScript needed for basic cases. These constraints appear as browser-native error messages.

<!-- required: field must be filled -->
<input type="text" name="name" required />

<!-- minlength / maxlength: character limits -->
<input type="text" name="username" minlength="3" maxlength="20" />

<!-- min / max: number ranges -->
<input type="number" name="age" min="18" max="120" />

<!-- pattern: custom regex -->
<input type="text" name="postcode" pattern="[A-Z]{1,2}[0-9]{1,2}[A-Z]? [0-9][A-Z]{2}" title="UK postcode format" />

<!-- type validation -->
<input type="email" name="email" required />
<input type="url" name="website" />
⚠️ Never rely solely on client-side validation! Always validate on the server too, because HTML constraints can be bypassed.
Custom Validation Messages
The title attribute adds a custom hint to the browser's native error message when pattern validation fails. The placeholder attribute gives users formatting hints before they type.

<label for="phone">Phone (format: 555-0100)</label>
<input
  type="tel"
  id="phone"
  name="phone"
  pattern="[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}"
  placeholder="555-0100"
  title="Please enter phone as: 555-0100"
  required
/>

exercises.question: Create a username input that: is required, has a minimum length of 3 and maximum of 15, only allows letters and numbers (pattern), and has a helpful placeholder.
exercises.solution:
<label for="username">Username</label>
<input
  type="text"
  id="username"
  name="username"
  required
  minlength="3"
  maxlength="15"
  pattern="[A-Za-z0-9]+"
  placeholder="e.g. coder123"
  title="Letters and numbers only, 3-15 characters"
/>
hints: minlength and maxlength set character limits
exercises.explanation: Combining multiple validation attributes creates robust client-side constraints. Always pair with server validation.

sections.content: Labels — The Most Critical Accessibility Feature

Every input must have an associated label. Screen readers announce the label when a field receives focus. Link them with matching for (on label) and id (on input) attributes. Alternatively, wrap the input inside the label element.

<!-- Method 1: for/id (recommended) -->
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" />

<!-- Method 2: wrap input in label -->
<label>
  Full Name
  <input type="text" name="fullname" />
</label>

<!-- Method 3: aria-label (when no visible label is possible) -->
<input type="search" aria-label="Search the site" />
Fieldset & Legend for Grouping
<fieldset> groups related form controls. <legend> provides a caption for the group. This is especially important for radio buttons and checkboxes.

<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Subscription Plan</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" /> Free
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro" /> Pro — $9/month
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="plan" value="enterprise" /> Enterprise
    </label>
  </fieldset>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Notification Preferences</legend>
    <label><input type="checkbox" name="notify" value="email" /> Email</label>
    <label><input type="checkbox" name="notify" value="sms" /> SMS</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
🎯 Using aria-describedby="hint-id" links a hint/error message to its input so screen readers announce both label and description.

exercises.question: Create a form with a fieldset for 'Account Type' containing two radio buttons: 'Personal' and 'Business'. Include a legend and proper labels for each radio.
exercises.solution:
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Account Type</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="account" value="personal" /> Personal
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="account" value="business" /> Business
    </label>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Next</button>
</form>
hints: Both radios need the same name
exercises.explanation: Fieldset + legend groups radio buttons so screen readers announce 'Account Type: Personal, radio button, 1 of 2' — without this, users just hear 'radio button' with no context.
